[Takeaways]{.cs-label}

- The county turnout model beats "same as the last midterm" in both backtests: 6.4 points of error against 10.5 in 2018, and 4.2 against 4.6 in 2022.
- Race polls halve the 2022 Brier score (0.067 to 0.031), but their 80% intervals caught only 77% of results. The most confident calls are probably overstated.

- The v1 forecast favours Democrats in the House (93%), narrowly in the Senate (63%) and for a majority of governorships (62%).

Turnout First is my forecast of the 3 November 2026 US midterms. It covers turnout in every county, the chance each side wins every Senate and governor race (71 in all) and all 435 House seats. It uses public data only. The forecast is a tagged Git commit with a timestamp, so it cannot be edited after the fact, and I will score it against the certified results.

Most public forecasts start with who wins. This one starts with how many people vote. The model forecasts national turnout of 47.9% of citizens of voting age, a little above 2022's 46.5%. Democrats reach 51 Senate seats in 63% of simulations and Republicans keep 50 or more in 33%. Democrats hold a majority of governorships (26 or more) in 62%, and win 218 or more House seats in 93%. The more useful finding is about the method: forecasting turnout first improves the county picture a great deal and changes the race forecasts very little.

**Source code**: [github.com/olivia-jackson-lambert/midterms-forecast-2026](https://github.com/olivia-jackson-lambert/midterms-forecast-2026) <!-- v1: add the link to the v1 tag (the repo is private until then) -->

# The Question

How many people will vote in each county on 3 November 2026? And given that, what is the chance each side wins each Senate, governor and House race?

I set the scope before building anything: county turnout as a share of citizens of voting age, with an 80% interval, and two-party vote share and win probability for every Senate and governor race. The House was a stretch goal. I added it on 13 October, once the rest was built, under the same backtest rule. Primaries, ballot measures and state legislatures are out of scope.

# Why Turnout First

Midterm turnout moves a lot. Measured against the voting-eligible population, it was about 37% in 2014 and 50% in 2018, then 46% in 2022. Presidential years move far less. A forecast that treats the electorate as fixed is ignoring the most variable part of a midterm.

Starting with turnout also gives the forecast something concrete to be wrong about. A county turnout map can be checked against certified results county by county, a much larger test than 71 races. And because each simulation draws turnout first, uncertainty about who votes carries through into the vote shares.

Whether turnout changes who is forecast to win was an open question. It turned out not to, and that result is below.

![How the forecast is built, from public data to the published numbers. Green boxes are fitted models.](assets/pipeline_overview.png){fig-alt="Flow diagram. Four sources at the top: election results from MIT precinct files, Wikipedia and states; ballots cast from the EAC survey and UF certified totals; Census citizens of voting age and ACS; and the generic ballot from aggregators since 1998. The first three feed an ingest and checks step covering 3,104 county units, using only values available by 1 October in every backtest. That feeds Stage A, the county turnout model. The generic ballot becomes the national House vote, corrected for bias using earlier cycles only. Stage A passes turnout-weighted leans to Stage B, the Senate and governor model for 71 races, which also takes the national vote. The national vote also feeds the House model for 435 districts. Race polls from Wikipedia are blended into Stage B. Stage B with polls and the House model feed 20,000 joint simulations, which produce county turnout, race probabilities and chamber control. All three outputs are checked against the 2018 and 2022 backtests." width="80%"}

# The Data

Every source is public and needs no API key or download form, except the FEC, which needs a free key.

| Need | Source |
|---|---|
| County presidential results, 2008 to 2024 | MIT Election Lab county returns (2008 to 2016); a county results mirror on GitHub (2020 and 2024) |
| Midterm ballots cast by county, 2014 to 2022 | EAC Election Administration and Voting Survey (EAVS) |
| Certified state totals and national turnout since 1980 | UF Election Lab (Michael McDonald) |
| Midterm county results, 2018 and 2022 | MIT Election Lab precinct returns, plus state sources for California and Tennessee in 2022 |
| Turnout denominator | Census citizen voting-age population (CVAP), the five-year vintage centred on each election |
| County demographics | American Community Survey 2020 to 2024 |
| Generic ballot, 1998 to 2026 | FiveThirtyEight's daily average; for 2026, the mean of five aggregators listed on Wikipedia |
| Races, nominees, incumbents and past results | Wikipedia's Senate, governor and House election pages, parsed from saved copies |
| Race polls, 2018 to 2026 | The poll tables in each race's Wikipedia article |
| Presidential results by House district | The Downballot and Daily Kos Elections public sheets, on the map in force each year |

Counties and results do not line up everywhere, so the model works on 3,104 county units. Alaska, Connecticut and DC are one unit each, and a few counties are merged where results and Census boundaries do not match, such as the three counties around Kansas City, which reports its results separately.

None of these sources could be used as downloaded. The main problems I found and fixed:

**Party labels and totals.** MIT's simplified party column is wrong for some nominees (in 2022 it labels Tim Walz in Minnesota as "other"), so votes are assigned by matching the nominees parsed from the race pages. Its total-votes column is wrong in places, so totals are summed from candidate votes. The GitHub mirror undercounts California, New York and Rhode Island by several million votes in 2012 and 2016, so it is only used for 2020 and 2024.

**EAVS gaps.** Alabama's 2014 figures are registrations, not ballots. Illinois 2014 is blank. Hawaii and Utah 2014 are off by about a third. Wisconsin 2018 and 2022 have no county codes. Every county figure is checked against two references and replaced where it fails, and each state is scaled to UF's certified total. Rows that had to be estimated (256 units in 2014, 5 in each later year) are never used for training.

**Leaks from the future.** It is easy to backtest with the final pre-election polling average, which a forecaster on 1 October would not have had. Every backtest here uses the generic ballot as it stood on 30 September, or the last archived value before it, and only race polls whose fieldwork ended by 26 September.

# The Turnout Model

The turnout model has two levels, fitted in PyMC.

**National.** Midterm turnout is the last presidential turnout minus a midterm drop, with the drop and its spread estimated from every midterm since 1986 before the target year. Out of sample since 1998, this beats "same as the last midterm" (logit error 0.19 against 0.23).

**County.** Each county's change from the last midterm depends on how far presidential turnout ran above that midterm, a pull back towards the county's average, a Senate race joining or leaving the ballot, the closeness of the top race, an out-party effect (county lean times a change in which party holds the White House), seven demographic slopes and a state effect. County noise is Student-t and grows for small counties. It is fitted on the 2014 to 2018 and 2018 to 2022 transitions.

![What drives the change in county turnout, as points of turnout for a typical difference between counties.](assets/turnout_drivers.png){fig-alt="Dot plot of twelve terms with 89% intervals, in points of turnout change. Presidential surge carried over is largest at plus 3.2. Pull back to average is minus 1.9. Senate race added is plus 1.3. Share aged 65 and over plus 0.8, share with a degree plus 0.7 and out-party lean plus 0.4 are also clearly positive. Population density, the shares of residents who are Hispanic or Latino and Black non-Hispanic, top race closer, median household income and share aged 18 to 29 all have intervals crossing zero. A note explains that the shares describe counties, not individual voters." width="88%"}

The strongest predictor is how much of the last presidential surge carries over. A county whose 2024 turnout ran well above its 2022 turnout tends to stay higher. A Senate race on the ballot adds about 1.3 points. Most demographic slopes are too uncertain to call either way.

Each of 20,000 simulations draws national turnout, then shifts every county by the same amount on the logit scale so that the national total matches.

One deviation from the plan: the out-party term was added after the first backtest showed a county-size bias that flipped sign between 2018 and 2022. Both versions are reported in the backtests, and the forecast uses the version with it.

# The Vote Model

The vote model forecasts the Democratic share of the two-party vote in each Senate and governor race, on the logit scale, as the sum of:

- the national House vote, drawn from the 30 September generic ballot with its historical bias and spread, estimated from earlier cycles only;
- the state's lean against the nation, from the last presidential result re-weighted county by county with the turnout forecast;
- incumbency, and the incumbent's track record: how their last result compared with what a uniform swing predicted;
- regional, same-state and race errors.

I call this the fundamentals forecast. Around 30 September the generic ballot has overstated the Democratic House vote in 11 of the 12 cycles since 1998, by 1.7 points on average, and the model corrects for that. The 2026 generic ballot of 54.7% two-party becomes a national House vote of 52.9% (80%: 51.3 to 54.5).

The errors are shared. Every simulation draws one national error, plus regional and same-state errors, so the model does not treat races as independent. Treating them as independent is the most common way a forecast becomes overconfident.

In Nebraska, Idaho and South Dakota the Senate race has no Democrat, and an independent challenger faces the Republican. The model treats the independent as it would a Democrat, with extra uncertainty, and a seat they win is not counted as Democratic.

An earlier version looked better in backtests than it should have: it used the final pre-election generic ballot and set error floors by looking at the 2022 backtest. I rebuilt it on the inputs above.

## Adding Polls

The fundamentals forecast knows nothing about the candidates beyond incumbency, which is the main reason it disagreed with published ratings in Texas, Ohio, Alaska and Iowa. So I added race polls as a separate layer on top.

**What.** For each race I take the poll tables from its Wikipedia article and keep only head-to-heads between the actual nominees. In the backtests a poll counts only if its fieldwork ended by 26 September. In 2026, 60 of 71 races have at least one qualifying poll. The rest are mostly safe seats, plus Florida, Colorado and Alaska governor, and keep the fundamentals forecast.

**How.** Each race gets a poll average: each pollster's latest poll, likely voters preferred, weighted towards recent polls (a 21-day half-life) and larger samples. The model treats that average as a noisy reading of the result. Polls miss in two ways: a national error that every race shares in a given year, and a race error that shrinks as polls accumulate. The size of each is fitted on earlier years only. In each simulation the forecast moves from the fundamentals towards the polls in proportion to how precise the polls are, with one national polling error drawn for every race at once. In 2026 the polls get a median weight of about 70%.

**The gain.** The rule was the same as for every other input: keep polls only if they improve the 2022 backtest on both Brier score and vote-share error. They do, by a lot. The 2022 Brier score falls from 0.067 to 0.031 and vote-share error from 3.6 to 2.7 points. In 2018, on priors alone, Brier falls from 0.149 to 0.062.

**The cost.** The intervals are now too narrow. With polls, the 80% intervals contained 77% of 2022 results and 71% of 2018's. Two elections are not enough to size the national polling error well, and widening the intervals until the backtests look right would be tuning to the test, the mistake that sank the earlier version. So I am leaving it and saying it plainly: the most confident calls are probably overstated. North Carolina's Senate race is the clearest case. The model gives Democrats 98%, on a poll average of 55.6% from 18 polls, while the published ratings call it Lean or Likely Democratic. I would read it as a clear favourite, not a near certainty, and the same goes for other races above 90%.

# Backtests

For 2018 and 2022, I fitted each model using only data available on 1 October of that year and scored it against the results. Each has a baseline to beat. The rule, set in advance: if the model did not beat its baselines, it would be published as an analysis, not a forecast.

## Turnout

| | 2018 | 2022 |
|---|--:|--:|
| Counties scored | 2,843 | 3,094 |
| Mean absolute error, model (points) | **6.4** | **4.2** |
| Same as last midterm | 10.5 | 4.6 |
| Weighted by population, model | **8.9** | **4.6** |
| Weighted, same as last midterm | 14.0 | 5.3 |
| 80% interval coverage | 96% | 89% |
| National turnout, 80% band | 38 to 48% | 44.5 to 56% |
| National turnout, actual | 50.9% | 46.5% |
| With national turnout known: error, coverage | 5.9, 99% | 3.9, 81% |

![County turnout error in each backtest, model against the same-as-last-midterm baseline.](assets/backtest_error.png){fig-alt="Dumbbell chart of mean absolute error in county turnout, in points. 2018, every county: model 6.4, baseline 10.5. 2018, weighted by population: model 8.9, baseline 14.0. 2022, every county: model 4.2, baseline 4.6. 2022, weighted by population: model 4.6, baseline 5.3. The model is lower in all four rows." width="88%"}

The model beats the baseline in both years, by a wide margin in 2018 and a modest one in 2022.

Most of the remaining error is national. The 2018 surge to 50.9% fell outside the model's national 80% band of 38 to 48%. With the national level known, the 2022 county intervals cover 81% of counties, close to the 80% they should. The 2018 intervals are too wide: there is no public county turnout for 2010, so that backtest had no earlier transition to learn from and ran on priors alone. Only 2022 tests the full county model, and two elections cannot say much about whether the national band itself is calibrated. It is wide on purpose.

The out-party term trades a little error for better intervals. Without it, 2022 error was 4.0 points instead of 4.2, but coverage with the national level known fell to 72%.

![Predicted against actual county turnout in 2022, for the baseline and the model.](assets/backtest_2022_scatter.png){fig-alt="Two side-by-side hexbin scatter plots of predicted against actual 2022 county turnout, both axes from 10 to 90%, with a dashed line marking perfect prediction. Left, same as last midterm, error 4.6 points: a broad cloud around the line. Right, the model, error 4.2 points: a slightly tighter cloud around the line." width="92%"}

Scored on races with a Democrat against a Republican: 68 in 2018 and 70 in 2022. The 2018 model ran on priors alone, since there were no earlier comparable midterms to fit on. The 2022 model was fitted on 2018.

| | 2018 | 2022 |
|---|--:|--:|
| Brier score, model with polls | **0.062** | **0.031** |
| Brier, fundamentals only | 0.149 | 0.067 |
| Brier, presidential lean called with certainty | 0.221 | 0.086 |
| Brier, lean plus uniform national swing | 0.162 | 0.157 |
| Vote-share error, model with polls (points) | **2.7** | **2.7** |
| Vote-share error, fundamentals only | 5.1 | 3.6 |
| Vote-share error, presidential lean | 5.9 | 4.3 |
| Vote-share error, uniform swing | 5.1 | 4.1 |
| 80% interval coverage, with polls | 71% | 77% |
| 80% interval coverage, fundamentals only | 96% | 86% |

![Race backtests: Brier score and vote-share error for the model with polls, the fundamentals alone and two baselines.](assets/race_backtest.png){fig-alt="Two dot plots comparing four forecasts in 2018 and 2022. Top, Brier score, lower is better: in 2018 the model with polls scores 0.062, fundamentals only 0.149, lean plus uniform swing 0.162 and presidential lean 0.221; in 2022 the model with polls scores 0.031, fundamentals only 0.067, presidential lean 0.086 and lean plus uniform swing 0.157. Bottom, vote-share error in points: in 2018 the model with polls is 2.7, while fundamentals only and uniform swing are both about 5.1 and presidential lean is 5.9; in 2022 the model with polls is 2.7, fundamentals only 3.6, uniform swing 4.1 and presidential lean 4.3." width="88%"}

The fundamentals alone beat both baselines on Brier score in both years, and on vote share they tie uniform swing in 2018 and beat it in 2022. Polls improve every score, and they are what the forecast uses.

![Calibration of race forecasts with polls, 2018 and 2022 pooled.](assets/race_calibration.png){fig-alt="Calibration plot of forecast chance Democrats win against the share of races it won, in five bins, with a dashed diagonal for perfect calibration. 53 races near 3% won none. 7 races near 30% won 1. 11 races near 51% won 7. 9 races near 71% won 6. 58 races near 96% won 57. The points sit close to the diagonal, with the two middle bins a little above and below it." width="65%"}

The ends of the scale are well calibrated: 111 races forecast below 20% or above 80% went the expected way in all but one. The 20 races between 40% and 80% went to Democrats 13 times, against about 12 expected. That is a small sample; the interval coverage above is the more telling number.

# The House

**Method.** The House model has the same structure as the vote model. Each district's lean is the 2024 presidential two-party share on the map in force for 2026; nine states redrew for 2026, including Texas, California, North Carolina and Ohio. The lean is moved by the same national House vote, plus incumbency and regional, state and district errors, fitted in PyMC on earlier midterms only. Each simulation draws the national vote and the errors, so districts in the same state move together. Two things from the vote model are left out. Turnout weighting would need a county-to-district split of every new map, which is not public, and it barely moves leans anyway. The incumbent's track record made the 2022 House backtest worse (Brier 0.035 against 0.031), so it failed the rule. Fifteen districts with candidates of only one party are counted as certain holds.

Scored on districts with a Democrat against a Republican (394 in 2018, 399 in 2022). Both baselines are called with certainty.

| | 2018 (priors only) | 2022 (fitted on 2018) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Brier score, model | 0.058 | **0.031** |
| Brier, presidential lean | 0.084 | 0.055 |
| Brier, lean plus uniform swing | **0.053** | 0.055 |
| Vote-share error, model (points) | 2.8 | **2.2** |
| Vote-share error, presidential lean | 3.5 | 3.2 |
| Vote-share error, uniform swing | 2.8 | 2.3 |
| 80% interval coverage | 99% | 91% |
| Democratic seats, actual | 234 | 213 |
| Model median (80% interval) | 228 (191 to 291) | 210 (195 to 225) |

In 2022 the model beats both baselines, though only narrowly against uniform swing on vote share (2.2 against 2.3 points), and the actual seat count fell inside its 80% band. In 2018, on priors alone, it does not beat uniform swing on Brier and its intervals are far too wide. Most of its edge comes from giving probabilities instead of certain calls. It passes the rule, and I present it with that caveat.

![Distribution of Democratic House seats across 20,000 simulations.](assets/house_seats_2026.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the chance of each number of Democratic House seats after the election, from about 202 to 287. Bars below 218 seats are red and bars from 218 are blue, with a dashed line between 217 and 218. The distribution peaks around 228 to 236 seats at about 3.5% each, with a long tail towards higher counts. Text reads Democrats win 218 plus: 93%, and median 234 seats, 80% interval 219 to 252." width="88%"}

**2026.** Democrats win a median of 234 seats (80%: 219 to 252) and 218 or more in 93% of simulations; Republicans reach 218 in 7%. Thirteen districts give Democrats between a 40% and 60% chance, and 50 between 20% and 80%.

**Known gaps.** Alaska and Maine are modelled on first-round shares, not the ranked-choice final round. Louisiana's new map holds a first round on 3 November with several candidates per party, modelled as the summed Democratic against Republican vote. Errors are shared only nationally, by region and by state, so districts that move together for other reasons are treated as independent within a state, and the seat interval may be a little narrow. And with 2018 running on priors, one midterm is a thin basis for the fitted slopes.

Republicans currently hold 53 seats. Democrats need 51 for control, since the Vice President breaks ties. Across 20,000 simulations:

| Republicans hold 50 or more seats | 33% |
| Neither, with independents holding the balance | 4% |

The most likely outcomes are 51 or 52 Democratic-caucus seats, close enough to the line that small shifts in a few races move the control odds a lot. Without polls the picture is reversed: Democrats reach 51 in 42% of simulations and Republicans hold 50 in 53%. Given the narrow intervals described above, 63% is probably a little too confident.

Thirty-six governorships are on the ballot. Republicans hold 26 governorships and Democrats 24, counting Virginia's change of party in 2025. Of the 14 not up this year, 6 are held by Democrats and 8 by Republicans. Democrats hold 26 or more in 62% of simulations, the two parties split 25 each in 17%, and Republicans keep a majority in 22%. The median is 26 Democratic governors (80%: 23 to 29).

Polls matter more here than in the Senate. Without them, Democrats reach 26 in 40% of simulations. The largest moves are Iowa (36% to 85% for Democrats), Michigan (64% to 92%) and Ohio (42% to 69%), against Georgia, which moves from 63% to 46%. The same caution about narrow intervals applies.

# What Turnout Does and Does Not Do

The case for forecasting turnout first was that a different electorate could change state leans. In practice it hardly does. Re-weighting each state's presidential result county by county with forecast turnout moves the lean by about 0.15 points on average across the 71 races, and by at most half a point.

The backtests agree. With the plain presidential lean instead of the turnout-weighted one, the 2022 Brier score of the fundamentals is 0.069 instead of 0.067, and 2018 is slightly better without it (0.147 against 0.149). That is a small edge in one year and none in the other.

So turnout does not decide who is forecast to win. Where it matters is the county forecast itself, which beats its baseline clearly, and the uncertainty: each race simulation draws a turnout scenario, so a high- or low-turnout year moves every lean together. I think that is a useful result to report. It is not the one I expected when I named the project.

# What Was Tested and Left Out

The rule for each: keep it only if it improves the 2022 backtest on both Brier score and vote-share error, against the fundamentals at 0.067 and 3.6 points.

![Every input tested, kept or left out under the same rule.](assets/what_was_tested.png){fig-alt="Two columns of boxes. Kept, in green: presidential surge carried over, the strongest turnout predictor; out-party lean, which raised 2022 interval coverage from 72% to 81%; Senate race on the ballot, about plus 1.3 points of turnout; incumbent track record, race Brier 0.072 to 0.067 in 2022; race polls, race Brier 0.067 to 0.031 in 2022; and turnout-weighted leans, a small edge in 2022 and none in 2018. Tested and left out, in dashed outline: fundraising, worse in 2022 at Brier 0.069 against 0.067; every nominee's track record, worse at 0.075 against 0.067; track record in the House, worse in the 2022 House backtest; early vote, untestable because no 2018 state data survive; special elections, with no comparable 2018 or 2022 series; and pundit ratings, never an input and used for comparison only." width="80%"}

**Fundraising.** I downloaded each Senate nominee's receipts from the FEC, using the June report, the last public before 1 October. It made both scores worse (Brier 0.069, error 3.7 points), so it is out. Once the state's lean, the national environment and the incumbent's record are in, money adds little. Well-funded challengers mostly run where the race was already close.

**Every nominee's track record.** The incumbent's track record helps: without it, the 2022 Brier score rises to 0.072. So I built the same measure for every nominee who had run statewide before, from their most recent Senate, governor or at-large House race since 2010. It made both scores worse (Brier 0.075, error 3.8 points), so it is out. A challenger's past result seems to be mostly their state's lean and the national mood of that year, which the model already has. It would have mattered: in the fundamentals forecast it moved Alaska Senate (Mary Peltola) from 20% to 35% for Democrats, and the Ohio special (Sherrod Brown) from 30% to 40%. Those are exactly the races where I would not want to lean on a feature that failed its test.

**Early vote.** The fair test compares each state's early-vote pace with its own pace at the same point in the previous midterm, since comparing states with each other mostly measures voting rules. I could not run it: no state-level figures from three weeks before the 2018 election survive, and only national totals for 2022. So early vote is out. I am now saving the 2026 figures every day to Election Day, so the test will be possible next cycle.

**Special elections.** Over-performance in special elections is a common signal of the national mood. It cannot be backtested here, because there is no comparable public series for 2017 to 2018 and 2021 to 2022. Several 2026 contests were also all-party ballots or Democrat against Democrat, which makes a two-party swing hard to define.

# Limits

**Two backtests.** Everything here is judged on 2018 and 2022, and 2018 ran on priors alone. That is enough to beat a baseline. It is not enough to know whether a 70% forecast wins 70% of the time.

**Intervals that are too narrow.** With polls, the race intervals covered 77% and 71% of results where they should cover 80%. The polling error is shared across races, so when polls miss, they tend to miss in the same direction everywhere. In 2022 they overstated Democrats by about 1.4 points on average.

**Independent candidates.** In Nebraska, Idaho and South Dakota the model treats the independent as it would a Democrat, with extra uncertainty, with no history of races like these to test that on. Where an independent runs alongside both nominees, as in Montana's Senate race, the polls' Democrat-against-Republican share ignores them, and the forecast there looks too sure.

**The national level dominates.** Most turnout error is national, and the national band is wide. A year like 2018 can fall outside it.

**Denominators are estimates.** CVAP is a survey estimate, so a handful of very small counties show turnout above 100%. Chattahoochee County, Georgia shows about 20% because Fort Moore's residents are counted there but mostly vote elsewhere.

**Demographics are fixed.** The model uses ACS 2020 to 2024 for every year, because the files I could use start with that vintage. Demographics change slowly and contain no results, but it is a departure from using only what was known at the time.

**Data parsed from Wikipedia.** Nominees, incumbents, polls and the 2026 generic ballot come from Wikipedia pages, checked against MIT's files where possible.

# Scorecard

The forecast will be scored after the election, once results are certified. The plan is to publish:

- forecast against result for every race and House district, with Brier score and log loss;
- county turnout error, and how often the actual turnout fell inside the 80% interval;
- calibration of the race forecasts, and how often results fell inside the 80% intervals;
- every miss, with what I think caused it.

This section will be filled in during the week of 9 November. <!-- scorecard: to come -->
